sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the region across the lower Reno River and Secchia River valleys and belongs to the Ferrara Arc thrust front. This fault system is the NE-verging external arc at the north-eastern tip of the Northern Apennines chain, well into the Po Plain, and marks the northeastern most advanced thrust with damaging seismogenic potential in the Apennines. This source has been updated within the research developed during the European Project GeoMol (http://www.geomol.eu/).
On 20 and 29 May 2012 two Mw 5.9 and 5.8 earthquakes and their aftershocks sequence hit the central Po Plain about 40 km north of Bologna. During the seismic sequence pure compressional faulting was generated by the blind thrusts of the western Ferrara Arc, thereby activating a 50 km-long stretch of this buried outer front of the Northern Apennines. The focal mechanisms of the larger shocks agree with the compilation of present-day tectonic stress indicators showing in the area a ca. N-S oriented maximum horizontal stress, i.e. oriented perpendicular to the main structural trends. Most of the seismic sequence was confined between 1 and 12 km depth, above the local basal detachment of the outer thrust front of the Northern Apennines.
Besides the 2012 earthquake sequence, historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a sparse intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) seismicity in the region, with the notable exception of the 22 Feb 1346 (Mw 5.8) Ferrara earthquake.
This Source is the main portion of the blind Romagna Apennines outer thrust and may account for the damaging seismicity of the region. In fact, subsurface data (e.g., Cassano et al., 1986) show well developed buried anticlines, including the Mirandola one. Also, there are well known drainage anomalies in this area (eg., Castaldini et al., 1979), for which Burrato et al. (2003) hypothesize a tectonic origin. The latter authors propose that segments of the blind thrusts imaged by the subsurface data may be potential sources of infrequent Mw 5.5+ earthquakes in this area.
A segment of this Source is the seismogenic source of the Mw 5.8, 29 May 2012 earthquake, second main shock of the 2012 sequence. For an in-depth analysis of seismogenesis in this region, the reader can refer to the Individual Source in this Database.
The strike of this Source was based on that of the mapped regional structures. The dip was based on geological observations and geometrical considerations. The rake represents pure thrusting based on geological observations. The minimum and maximum depth were based on tectonic and geometrical considerations concerning the thrust geometry. The slip rate was based on geological observations from Maesano et al. (2015).

pictures.t: Tectonic map of the Northern Apennines thrust fronts
pictures.c: Structural map of the Northern Apennines thrust fronts showing a temporal reconstruction of their activity (from Castellarin et al. [1985]).

pictures.t: River anomalies and buried anticlinal axes in the Po Plain
pictures.c: Map showing the position of the main drainage anomalies in the Po Plain compared with the axes of buried anticlines of the Northern Apennines fronts (from Burrato et al. [2003]). The seismogenic source of the 1624 Argenta earthquake falls to the north of the anomaly nr. 22 related to the Idice River.
Geologic cross-section across Mirandola anticline (from Scrocca et al. [2007]).

pictures.t: Vertical movements in the Po Plain near Mirandola
pictures.c: Summary of inferred Holocene vertical movements in the area of the Panaro, Secchio and Po rivers, near Mirandola (from Panizza et al. [1987]).

pictures.t: Paleochannels of the Po River and main tributaries
pictures.c: Recent evolution of the Po River and its main tributaries. The thrust fault driving the Mirandola anticline is likely responsible for the attraction of the Panaro and Secchia rivers towards the syncline north of Modena, while the Po River appears to be shifted northward (from Veggiani [1985]).

pictures.t: Geological cross-section across Northern Apennines fronts
pictures.c: Geological cross-section showing structural architecture of the Northern Apennines thrust fronts. The lower section is a restoration for early Pleistocene (from Picotti and Pazzaglia [2008]).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).

pictures.t: Radarsat differential interferogram of the 2012 sequence
pictures.c: Radarsat-1 interferogram showing the coseismic ground uplift produced by the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes. The pattern of upift highlights the geometrical en-echelon relationships between the two seismogenic sources, and the vertical ground deformation of the Mirandola anticline. The simplified geological section shows the geometry at depth of the thrust fault source of the 29 May 2012 shock (from Bignami et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Cosmo-Sky Med interferograms of the 2012 sequence
pictures.c: COSMO-SkyMed interferogram and coseismic ground displacement maps of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes. The red stars show epicenters of the M > 5 shocks occurred during the seismic sequence (from Salvi et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the Po Plain and its fluvial systems
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch showing the relationship between epicenters of the mainshocks of the 2012 seimic sequence, seismogenic sources of the DISS database and tectonic induced drainage anomalies (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Drainage anomalies in the epicentral area of the 2012 sequence
pictures.c: Declaration of a tectonic induced drainage anomaly: the buried Mirandola anticline induces the diversion of the Secchia and Panaro rivers (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Simplified geological section across 2012 epicentral area
pictures.c: Simplified geological section crossing the Mirandola anticline and the outer Ferrara Folds, and showing the proposed hypocenters of the two main shocks of the 2012 seismic sequence (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Drainage evolution of the central-southern Po Plain
pictures.c: Drainage evolution in the Po Plain south of the Po River. Tectonic growth of the buried Ferrara Folds induced the shift of the Secchia, Panaro, Reno and Po rivers. Drainage sudden diversions of the Po River in Guastalla (G) and Ficarolo (F) were controlled by major flood events after tectonic activity cumulated enough ground deformation (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Web based macroseismic intensities of the 29 May 2012 earthquake
pictures.c: Preliminary map of the macroseismic effects (MCS) of the 29 May 2012 earthquake (http://www.haisentitoilterremoto.it/). The data were collected using a web interface and were elaborated following the method proposed by Sbarra et al., 2010.

pictures.t: Compound macroseismic intensities of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes
pictures.c: Map of the cumulated macroseismic intensities (EMS) of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes (from Tertulliani et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the 2012 seismic sequence
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch of the 2012 seismic sequence with geological profile. Note that the coseismic deformation of the ground-surface caused by the 2012 sequence is consistent with the characteristic of the two 2012 seismogenic sources (from Vannoli et al. [2015]).
